utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Wednesday, and I greet our witness, representatives of the OTP, and Mr. Seselj, as well as everyone helping us around this courtroom. We're now going to continue with the cross-examination of this witness. The Registrar told me that Mr. Seselj had one hour and two minutes left. Does the Prosecution want to ask anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. Your Honour, just before starting, I've just received two documents which Mr. Seselj intends to use, obviously, during his cross-examination. According to what is mentioned on the -- these are documents that -- these are faxes that we received yesterday, around 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning, but I only obtained them today. So I raise an objection regarding their use today, since they were disclosed too late. It is true that sometimes there are mishaps and documents that were forgotten, but regarding this witness, we didn't obtain a single document, so this is why I raise this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, obviously we have documents 6 and 7 on our table, and the fax shows that you obtained them yesterday at 7.48 in the morning. I fully understand that you arrived in the courtroom yesterday at 8.30 a.m. and you didn't have enough time, maybe, to take a look at these documents. I note that regarding document 7, you have studied it, since some paragraphs have been earmarked, five paragraphs have been earmarked, which means that you did take a look at these documents. Maybe you looked at it yesterday in the afternoon, I don't know, and maybe this is why we are only given this document this morning. Could you please explain what you've done with these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there probably is a way for the Registry to at least give you a record of the number of pages that I received by fax. I get more pages than I actually use. For instance, I have two statements by Vojin Vuckovic, Zuco. Both came in yesterday. I will only be using one. I will not use the other one because it deals with some scandal involving Kuwaiti dinars, and Zuco claims that Mr. Alic was involved. But this is of no interest to me, because it has nothing to do with war crimes, although his claims are quite interesting when it comes to the funding of the purchase of weapons for the Party of Democratic Action. I have to say something. I remained in the courtroom until 1.15. I wait for about an hour to get transported to the prison, and I can only start working until I get, once I get to the Detention Unit. I have some sports activities, I have to go for a walk, I have to talk to my associates, and what can I do? I get it in the morning and then I submit it to the Prosecution, and they claim it was not on time. Why don't they give me things on time? I found out that the Prosecution interviewed Vojin Vuckovic, Zuca, as a suspect. Why was I never given Zuca's statement? For months, we've had victims, witnesses, testifying about their ordeal in Zvornik. It's all about the Yellow Wasps. The commander of the Yellow Wasps gave a comprehensive statement to the Prosecution, and the Prosecution never told me about that. And I hear from Zuca directly yesterday that he gave this interview to the Prosecution, and now it is my fault for the Prosecution that I'm late by one day. And the fact that the Prosecution fails to disclose anything that is relevant to me, that's nobody's fault. It's the usual practice in all the cases. The Prosecution is not held accountable for what they do. Every time a Prosecution calls a false witness, for instance 007 or the one testifying before him, the one who threw grenades at Belgrade mosques, the Prosecution should be sanctioned, each and every time. In every legal system, it is impermissible for the Prosecution to prep their witnesses for years and then to have this kind of fiasco, and now the Prosecution is criticising me for being late for one day. I cannot give something to the Prosecution before I've studied it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, several things. Once again, you are talking about false witnesses. Each time you mention these false witnesses, this raises havoc in this courtroom. I've told you over and over that the Trial Chamber will only determine itself on the probative value of the witnesses in the end. Witnesses come, they are heard, they say things, you challenge what they're saying. Very well. Other witnesses come and testify either in your favour or against you. But it's only in the very end that we will decide. So the Trial Chamber is telling you, once again, not to mention false witnesses. You've already said this once. We've heard you. Fine, but remember that we assess the witnesses as they come, listening to you, of course, but we don't necessarily decide that they're false witnesses. You might be right, you might be wrong, but as of today, it is totally impossible for anyone to say this person is a false witness, 100 per cent sure. You know just as well as I do that the consequences of this are huge. If it is proven that a witness, under oath, lied, this witness risks a contempt procedure. So, please, sometimes, you know, you fly off the handle and say things very quickly, but pleases try to think twice and not to be so bold about these false witnesses, because this just creates problems every time. On the other hand, you have said something which I believe is very serious and which might have consequences, and I have to turn to the Prosecution. Mr. Seselj just told us a few minutes ago that regarding Zuco, the accused suddenly found out, through the written statement of this Zuco which Mr. Seselj received, that this Zuco had been heard by the OTP as a suspect. Having been heard as a suspect, this should have been disclosed to Mr. Seselj. So what happened exactly, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, and to Mr. Seselj and everyone in and around the courtroom. We are, as I speak, checking the records concerning any possible statements that this person, Mr. Vuckovic, Zuco, gave to the Prosecution, and hopefully we'll be able to determine that in just a moment. On the broader issue, of course, of suspect interviews, we are doing everything we possibly can to get those interviews transcribed and translated into the Serbian language. As I've indicated before, there are a number of resource and logistical issues concerned with that. We are working as diligently as we can to provide all such suspect interviews, many of which have never been transcribed before. I do, however, want to place on the record one other concern the Prosecution has with respect to the issue that the Presiding Judge raised concerning allegations of false witnesses. I'm not going to go into this in any elaborate detail, but I will put on the record that the Prosecution position is that that, in and of itself, is a form of intimidation with respect to future potential witnesses. And so it's not simply an issue of whether the Trial Chamber should be making any kind of determinations at this point. As the Presiding Judge clearly indicated, all the evidence will be weighed at the end. And of course, it is potentially serious if witnesses were found to be less than truthful during their testimony. That is also a separate issue. But we are very concerned about statements being made by the accused concerning false testimony or false witnesses because of the impact that such allegations may have on future witnesses. And for that reason, we also want it placed on the record our position, the Prosecution's position, that that is a form of witness intimidation, and it must be stopped. And we are very grateful for the Trial Chamber's comments that have been made in that respect, but I do want to put that on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, Mr. Mundis has addressed two points. First, he's looking in his database to see whether or not this Zuco was interviewed as a suspect. As soon as they know, of course, they will tell us about it. Now, regarding the second item, this is not the first time that the Prosecutor has been saying this. Mrs. Dahl before him also said that, and others said that before. When you say that witnesses to come are false witnesses, this has consequences. Just imagine for one second, Mr. Seselj, that Mr. Mundis would be saying that all witnesses -- all your Defence witnesses are false witnesses. You would be the first one to protest, and justly so, if the Prosecutor was claiming that, but you keep accusing the Prosecution witnesses of being false witnesses, quote/unquote. What consequences does this have? Well, for the witnesses to come, when they're reading the papers, when they're following the trial on TV, they keep -- they think, "Well, the accused thinks I'm going to be a false witness," and this could very well have a consequence on the testimony given by these people, and the Trial Chamber has drawn your attention to this on several occasions, on many occasions, actually; notably, the fact that the Prosecution could also allege that your witnesses are also in the same category. This is really an issue, so please refrain from saying this, because this has grave consequences. I fully understand that for your part, in your opinion, you believe that the witnesses that have testified up until now, according to you, lied regarding this or that. You can say it. In your submissions, you can write it also. You can say it, you can ask for a private session, but please do not say this in open session. This has consequences on the witnesses to come, whoever they may be and whoever's side they may be on; Prosecution, Defence. There could be consequences. Of course, in the heat of the moment, sometimes you get a head up and say this. It's true you've been waiting years for your trial, and I fully understand that sometimes it's hard to stay in control when you absolutely want to say things, but this is a technical issue. Witnesses come here. They make the solemn declaration. If they lie, they run the risk of being accused of contempt charges. As I told you, when a witness came, testified, if you had elements that could challenge what he said on a number of issues, you can just make a submission under Rule 77. You can always do that, but do this after the fact. Don't just do this when the witnesses are here. Now you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, I'm never hasty in what I say and I'm never impassioned. I am old enough to be somewhat bereft of passion, and I have never been hasty. I am frankly concerned that the Prosecution might call Defence witnesses publicly false witnesses, but I'm prepared to bear it. I am quite happy, despite this concern, that the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution are in such agreement on this issue. What you are saying about the Rules, as a principle, it would be fine, were it not for the fact that our practice is different here. Less than a month ago, you had a protected witness here with all the protective measures. I will not be saying his name. He admitted to the Prosecution that he had given false testimony in another case. And then you brought duty Defence counsel here for him and you prevented me from cross-examining him on this issue, lest he should repeat the fact that he had given false testimony. A month is gone, and there are no sanctions against this man, no indictment has been issued. I can see now that some journalist who disclosed names of protected witnesses have been indicted, deliberately or by accident. There are quite a few journalists on such charges. Some were tried before this Court. And a witness who admits that in a previous case, he had given false testimony, is gets away with it with impunity. And now you tell me there are protection mechanisms in place against such witnesses, and I don't believe you because I can see that they are not being applied, at least not in this case. We had a witness here who admitted to the Prosecution that he had testified in a previous case falsely. I will not mention his name, because you know that he testified in closed session for a week. You know who that is. And what am I to do, take your word that this is how it is going to be? On what basis? I cannot take anyone's word for it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let me answer you without giving a name, of course, because it's a protected witness. There is a witness who said something in front of another Trial Chamber, and in front of this Trial Chamber he had a different story. And you are absolutely right, this was noted. I told you that our Trial Chamber, this Trial Chamber, is not competent in the matter. The competent Trial Chamber is the other one. We do not have jurisdiction here. By definition, when this person gave us his own version on this issue, it's the truth he told us. He did not lie to us. Since he did not lie to us, why would we launch any kind of proceedings against this person? However -- and I've already told you this. However, regarding the other Trial Chamber, you can seize this other Trial Chamber, and so can the Prosecution. It's your problem and the problem of the Prosecutor. It is not our problem, because this witness told his truth in front of us, unless he lied to us again, which that would mean that he told the truth to the other Chamber. There is only one Trial Chamber that can have jurisdiction, and as things stand, it is not ours. I've already told you this, so please do not say that we are endorsing situations. I told you that -- I even told you that it's up to you to follow suit and take appropriate action. I mean, you could make a motion to the other Trial Chamber, explaining your problem. But I repeat, we are not competent in this matter. As you know, just as I do, the Trial Chamber only has the competence it was awarded, and in this case we are not competent to rule on this potential contempt case, which may come from the fact that he said that he gave another version of what he said to us in front of another Trial Chamber. First thing. So if your allegations of false testimony rely on this, it is not sufficient. Once again, regarding the words "false witnesses," we know you told me openly during the pre-trial phase -- you explained at length that in the Milosevic trial, according to you, some witnesses gave false testimonies. You actually said that they were totally remotely controlled through their headset and so on. You repeated this in your pre-trial submission. We know this, so there's no need to mention this again. Raising this matter again has consequences on the witnesses to come, and there's quite a number of these witnesses to come. We will now move to the cross-examination. You have one hour and two minutes left. If you have any other item to raise, please do it now, before you start with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very briefly. Mr. President, you're quite right, this witness that we were talking about testified truthfully for three days, to the satisfaction of the Prosecution and of the Trial Chamber. The only person lying here was me, in the cross-examination. I lied all the time, and he spoke the truth and nothing but the truth. I agree with you fully. You are completely right. But when we learned, all of us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, maybe there's a problem with the translation. I never said that this witness, this protected witness, had said the entire truth. I only said that on the specific item, if I remember well, that dealt with his military booklet, he gave us explanations on this. This is what I'm saying. So, please, do not -- I said one thing, and don't believe that I have -- that this can be extended to his entire testimony. Maybe it was a problem with the translation, but I just wanted to say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, quickly, just to make things very clear, nothing is preventing you and no one has prevented you in this Trial Chamber from challenging the credibility of a witness and using the correct procedure, which you have to follow. You can't demonstrate that a witness is lying on a certain item, on a fact, on a specific fact. However, what we cannot accept is that you make general statements regarding past and future witnesses, statements that would not be supported by evidence demonstrated in this courtroom during your cross-examination. This is extremely simple. No one is preventing you from demonstrating that a witness is not credible. It's up to you. It's up to you to be clever enough to do this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, we had in this courtroom a witness for whom it had been ascertained that he had lied in another case. There is an obligation on the part of every citizen to report any crime that he or she learns of. In this courtroom, the Judges learned about that, the Prosecution was aware of that, the Registry was aware of that, and so was I. Each and every Judge is duty-bound to report a crime if they learn that the crime has been committed. The Prosecution is under the obligation to immediately prosecute the person responsible, yet the Prosecution failed to do that. I'm the only one who is not under this obligation. I am a convict here, and the convict does not have the obligation to report crimes. And I don't want to go into this issue any further, because I can see that Mr. Alic is getting impatient on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we listen to everything you say, and very often what you're saying is based on legal foundation, and you've just raised one item. You've said that any citizen, when he is aware of an offence, must absolutely tell this to the authorities. This is something that exists in all jurisdictions. You're absolutely right. Secondly, false testimonies are ruled by Rule 77. Rule 77 calls for sanctions to be implemented by two authorities; either the Prosecutor, who will write out an indictment, or the Trial Chamber itself, who can write up an indictment, but only as far as it is competent, it's ration immateriae competent. And I told you that this Chamber is not competent in this case. The only body that can launch the sanctions here is the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor can seize the other Chamber, the other Trial Chamber. But yourself, as a potential victim of this, could also send a submission to the other Trial Chamber. Now, maybe there's a failing in the Rules regarding this. Maybe you believe that Judges should play a role in relation to the other Trial Chambers. Maybe you are correctly interpreting this loophole in the Rules. But as it is, as the Rules stand now, this is not clearly stated. We fully understood what you said. We will think about it together on the Bench, but as the Rule stands it is up to the Prosecution to draw up an indictment, possibly, or it is up to you to make a submission and send this submission to the competent Chamber. You said that you didn't want to waste the witness's time, so now you have the floor to continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, during the war, did you receive any decorations?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many decorations did you receive?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which decorations?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In 1987, I received a decoration in Serbia, a pistol with a plaque, from the Municipal Secretariat for the Interior at that time. And the second decoration or commendation was in 1994, from the Federal Minister of Internal Affairs, and that was a police badge, a silver police badge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the document from the Centre of Research into Crimes against the Serbian People. It's document 2. We started with that yesterday, and I read out the accompanying letter at the insistence of the Prosecutor, so let's take a look at that document together, Mr. Alic, and I'd like to hear your views as to parts of its contents. I don't have to read the first paragraph again. I think I read it out yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But just tell me whether you knew about these instructions to send candidates to the educational training centre of Croatia, signed by Hasan Cengic, MUP of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you tell me what year that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't know what the year was exactly. They were the war years, anyway. Now, which particular year, I can't say. Do you know anything about that? If not, we're not going to dwell on it.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the cadres of the Muslim MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina were sent for training and education to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know about that, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, in paragraph 2 of this document -- do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says the following about you: "Sometime in the second half of March 1992, he staged an incident which reverberated not only in the Tuzla region but in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. At night, he sounded the alarm as if the police station had been attacked and called in only the Muslim policemen to defend it." Did you do that in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there another alarm sounded?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was some rally -- there was a rally, but not an alarm sounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how come in March policemen rallied together and they happened to be only the Muslim members?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were Serbs, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when the Serbs withdrew from the police station and went to Karakaj, one Serb remained there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you mentioned his name. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: His name was Boro Zekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then you sent him packing because you didn't need him in the police station, either?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what happened to him, then? Did he stay on working with you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He asked to stay and work there, but we didn't stay on, either. We were expelled, too, from the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You fled on the 8th of April because you were defeated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the interpreters are asking you to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You stayed on, working at the police station, until the 8th of April, when you fled, because the Serb forces were stronger, there was discord among your ranks, you had internal conflicts, the chief of the War Staff fled, the mayor fled, and general chaos broke loose, and you left too. Now, I'm not accusing you for having left. It's better that you left and stayed alive, rather than being killed, because I wouldn't have anyone to talk to here in the courtroom now. However, this man, Boro Zekic, was forced out earlier, before the 8th of April; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Serb police left on the 6th of April. It separated and went to Karakaj on the 8th of April. The town of Zvornik was attacked from the 6th to the 8th. How long is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Two days.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right, two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And why, on the six 6th of April, did you send Boro Zekic packing when he wanted to work with you there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's not correct, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is true, then?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's true that Boro stayed alone and he wanted to see a united police force. However, Boro didn't want to go to war. He didn't -- and he said, "I don't belong up there. I don't want any war. Asim, I can't stay here, either, because I would have been considered a traitor of the Serb people." And I said, "Boro, go home. I'll write it as if you're on furlough, on annual leave. You'll see if this goes on -- well, you'll see how things develop and decide."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Boro went on holiday, his annual leave; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's right, he went on annual leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine, Mr. Alic. Now, it says here that the alarm that was sounded, that caused just the Muslim section of the police force to rally, although you said there were Serbs, too. My information tells me that there were no Serbs and that Mr. Ivanisevic also doesn't say that there were any Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well your information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Maybe it's not, maybe your information is correct. Anyway, Mr. Ivanisevic goes on to say here as to your file that this led to a revolt on the part of those employed, even some Muslims, who were honest and decent professionals in their job. At a heated meeting that was held after that, representatives from Tuzla came and assistant Minister of Internal Affairs Muharem Saric came from Sarajevo; is that correct? Did Muharem Saric come from Sarajevo in March 1992 to Zvornik? Did he come to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know any Muharem Saric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Assistant Minister for internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, the man doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what about police officials from Tuzla, did they arrive?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I interrupted you because I've noticed something. When the interpreters translate what you are saying directly from Serbian into French in realtime, I can follow what you're saying, and I also get the answers of the witness. But when what you are saying is translated into English and there's a time lag in the translation, as has just occurred, you then continue speaking in your language, and the interpreter is translating into English, which means that if I want to be in realtime, I need to look at the screen and read the English, when you have already addressed another topic. This is why it's difficult. I've already mentioned this to the interpreters. I would like you to be interpreted directly from Serbian into English. They're doing their best, anyway. In this particular instance today, please go more slowly so that there is no time lag. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll do my best to speak as slowly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says here, Mr. Alic, that Serb policemen reacted especially in a heated manner, and that was the reason that they left the police station and went to Kalesija. Well, that is an assumption. Now, tell me, what did those representatives of the Tuzla Centre of the Security Service do, then, when they came to Zvornik with respect to this problem? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mentioned Kalesija?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I didn't mention Kalesija. I meant "Karakaj." They went to Karakaj, not Kalesija, although Kalesija was under Serb control for a time and then the Muslims managed to seize control of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, as the accused has mentioned himself, he's asked the witness to speculate who has said, well, this is an assumption, and I object to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your objection is on the record now. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking the witness to speculate. What I'm asking the witness is to explain to us, here and now, to everyone, what these police representatives from Tuzla, where the Security Service Centre to which Zvornik belonged, how they arrived, and they arrived because of the problem that was going on there. And I read out a portion from Mr. Ivanisevic's statement that Mr. Alic complained --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sounded the alarm, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and that he had not sounded any alarm but that the rally was spontaneous. Then I said that only the Muslim part of the police station rallied together, and then he said there were Serbs, too, although he couldn't name anybody. And then he said that high-ranking police representatives from the Tuzla center arrived and then my question was without any cause for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What did they do in Zvornik, once they arrived?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: May I be allowed to clarify? In view of the fact that people knew much earlier on, and had been checked out, we had reliable information telling us that in Celopek a review of the then Serb police was carried out, had been carried out, and the review had been carried out by Dragan Spasojevic, the commander of the police station at the time. The leadership in the Security Centre knew about this. We were informed of that fact. Now, afterwards, after we say this small incident, I called upon the representatives of the Security Centre to come to Zvornik to hold a joint meeting there and to try to convince the Serbs that we should remain together in a united police force and that it should continue to be a united police force. So that was the reason for their arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You managed to persuade them, I see.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After a day or two, unfortunately -- well, that was their intention before. It was just a matter of time, when they would be displaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And your leadership in Sarajevo asked the European Union to recognise the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what they asked for up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the European Union, precisely on the 6th of April, recognised the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't deal with things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what happened on the 6th of April, 1941?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, tell us, then, so that we hear of that.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't want to go into that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you are duty-bound to answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And I have answered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you said that you knew what had happened on the 6th of April, 1941, and now you have to state what it was that happened. Otherwise, the Court will sanction you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened on the 6th of April, 1991 [as interpreted] -- 1941? Do you know or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume it was some sort of pretext for the war or cause for the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, I'm asking you what happened on the 6th of April, 1941.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know what happened and you've graduated from many schools. You don't know that Belgrade was bombed on that day and that is how Yugoslavia was pulled into World War II? How don't you know that, that Belgrade was bombed on the 6th of April? That is taught in primary school.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that that was a cause for some sort of war. It wasn't the pretext or cause, it was the beginning of the war as far as Yugoslavia was concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well then I agree. Quite obviously the European Union picked the 6th of April to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina precisely because that was the date of Hitler's aggression against Yugoslavia and the serious bombing of Belgrade; isn't that right? That's quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, very well. Now, do you know where the village of Rozanj is located?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 2nd of July, 1992, there was an attack by Muslim forces against that village?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How don't you know that when you took part in that attack?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was the chief of the civilian police force, and the civilian police force had no role in any combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, at that time wasn't the 206th Brigade of the Muslim Army already formed at that time or, rather, the BH Army, as you called it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It probably was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Didn't you, together with that brigade, with a portion of the policemen who were under your control, take part in the attack village of Rozanj?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where is the village of Rozanj, where is it located?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The village of Rozanj is located in the Sapna Municipality at the foot of Mount Meris [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So as the chief of police, you were in charge of that village, too?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Since there was no civilian population there, I had nothing to look for there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So if the Serbs were there, it's the same thing as if there were no civilians, but Serb civilians, Mita Rostec [phoen], Bogosav Ivic, Stanko Ostojic, Goran Ostojic and Nedeljka Ostojic, were killed there, and you've never heard of that, Mr. Alic; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was military security that dealt with things like that exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ah. Well, you see, Mr. Ivanisevic says on page 3 - turn to page 3 of the document, please - he says responsible for the crimes, the following were mentioned: Avdo Halilovic Grahorac, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Avdo Halilovic Grahorac.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the name rings a bell, but I don't know who it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Huso Avdic is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Ismet Halilovic is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that they're all people from the area, judging by the names, but I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know Sabit Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know Jure Juric, "Bonze" [phoen]? I suppose "Bonze" is his nickname. That's a Croat, is it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, there are no Croats up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, there were in Tuzla, of course, and were and there are today, too. But you're not talking about Tuzla, you're talking about Sapna?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm talking about the people that attacked that Serb village and killed the civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I object to questions being asked on this topic. The witness clearly said he knew nothing about this event. When questioned about a series of names, he said he didn't know these. I don't see in what manner it is relevant to put questions about this. Several times, he said he wasn't involved and knew nothing about this, so how often will these questions be repeated and put to the witness when he's told oftentimes -- said oftentimes that he knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that he wasn't there. He said he'd heard of a number of names, but the other names, he doesn't know. Do you wish to pursue the matter and do you want him to say, "No, no, no," every time, or are you going to move on to another topic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness denied his own participation in the attack against the Serb village of Rozanj and said that the village was to be found in the territory of Sapna, and that he didn't know of the attack on that village on the 2nd of July, 1992. The witness said all that, so I'm no longer asking you about the attack. I have information here about people, and their names, who took part in the attack and killed Serb civilians, so I have to go through the names and read the names out one by one to ask the witness whether he knows them. If it is established at the end that he doesn't know any of these people, then that answer satisfies me to a high degree. But why must I disclose the intentions of my cross-examination in advance? As soon as the witness finds himself in a difficult position, somebody intervenes again. Now the witness has regained his composure, so I can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know Ismet Omerovic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was he in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was from Godus, and he was one of the local commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The commander of what?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think he was in the battalion of the 206th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know Zijad Omerovic, nicknamed "Joja"?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he performed some duty, he had some post in that battalion, probably. But let me repeat again that that was a military formation, they were military operations, and I have nothing to do with those military operations. My work was from the remit of the civilian police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm not conducting your trial and we are not seized for what happened in that village which was under your authority, since you were in charge of the civilian police, but there's one thing which I cannot overlook, and you know this as well as I do. When, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the state of war was declared, the law was amended and specified that the civilians could be subordinated to the military units, and the policemen who were working for the Ministry of the Interior could be subordinated to military units. Therefore, when you say that this is a military matter, I might disagree with you. Nothing tells me that a military operation, particularly at the time when the Territorial Defence existed, the ABiH hadn't been entirely set up and formed yet, all the corps and units had not been formed, but there were military operations ongoing and ordered by the TO, sometimes by War Presidencies of the municipalities. And the civilian police could be incorporated into a military unit. Let me remind you of this. Now, can you confirm that in this military operation on this village, you did not take part in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know that the police may be resubordinated to the army, but at that time and in that place, there was no need for that, in light of the fact that Sapna Municipality covers a very small territory. It's maybe 30 per cent of what used to be Zvornik Municipality. And only the military was active in that area. I was the police chief with maybe 35 to 40 police officers under me, and we performed our normal duties; protecting people's lives and property and dealing with other civilian duties and needs, as much as it could be done. There was no need for us to be resubordinated because we were not a major force. We did not have appropriate weapons, and we did not take part in those operations. Only the army was there. When Mr. Seselj mentioned some names, I know these people were there, but the military was operating in that area. We had nothing to do with it. We couldn't even get access to those villages because they had village guards, before those villages were cleansed. We went into those villages after they were cleansed in order to protect property against looters, but we didn't participate in any combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, do you know who Muzijet Ramic is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you can keep mentioning names to me for as much as you want. Some names are familiar to me, some are not, but I don't know these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, well, the simplest thing would be to say "yes" or "no." If you say, "Yes," I'll ask you more details. If you say, "No," we'll go on.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think we're wasting your precious time on things that I cannot really confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why are you bothered about me wasting time? I have as much time as I have, as I want. I've been here for six years. I can be here for six years more.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's your decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know Zihad Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Serif Omerovic is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He's a villager from the village of Godus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was he in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think he was in the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the Civilian Protection was involved in a military operation and the police was not. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Civilian Protection had its specific role. It was not involved in military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the Civilian Protection performed a special, specific role by protecting the Serb civilians, by killing them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that isn't true at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Izet Jukic is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Alija Ramic is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Ferid Kundic is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I said already, you can say these names for three days and I don't know these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Semsudim Muminovic is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of the 206th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you can see this is what it says in the document?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't see it in front of me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the speakers to slow down and make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Sejfo Nekir is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nekir is probably his last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are quoting names which are not recorded on the transcript, since there is an indication that the name is missing. So, please, if quote names, quote them slowly so that these can be recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was under the impression that I did slow down in asking my questions. We are talking about Sejfo Nekir. Sejfo is his name, Nekir is his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic doesn't know him?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know Ferid Kajic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know Haris Begic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know Halil Smajlovic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know Hajrudin Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You saw your name is here in bold letters, "Asim Alic." Do you see that on the document?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please move it up a little bit for the benefit of Mr. Alic. That's in line 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the basis of the investigations carried out by this centre that is led by Mr. Milivoj Ivanisevic, the names of the people who are mentioned as perpetrators as crimes are listed here, and your name is here. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, and I can say with full responsibility that this has nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who is this Ivanisevic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ivanisevic is the head of the centre for the investigation of crimes against the Serb people. It is an institution that studies crimes against the Serbian people in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Mr. Ivanisevic has already published the products of his research in seven or eight books.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who appointed him and where is the headquarters? It is in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And he in Belgrade knows what happened there in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he carries out research?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, fine, fine, but this has -- this makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where Rastosnica is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it in the Sapna area?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know about the attack on Rastosnica on the 1st of September, 1992; have you heard of it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that 38 Serb civilians were killed in this attack?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know that there was an attack?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you don't know about the Serbs that were killed in the attack?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know about that because the military did that, and if there were civilian casualties, if there were, and I cannot say either way, then the military exchanged dead civilians on the one side for dead Muslim civilians or captured -- or prisoners of war for prisoners of war. It was all within their purview. We didn't have anything to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But, Mr. Alic, you said in your statement that you took part in the exchange of Serbs under your control for Muslims held by Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How big was this exchange?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was just one case where an old lady with a child remained there. At first, I was able to provide police protection, but she expressed a wish to go to Zvornik, and we did it, we met her wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, do you know about the attack at Rastosnica? You do. In the course of this attack carried out by the Muslim Army, a certain number of Serbs were captured. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I've told you already that this was all done by the army. They captured people, they exchanged people. They did that. We had nothing to do with that, no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, they brought them to Sapna when they picked them up in Rastosnica; is that correct? You were able to see them in the street as they were being led by?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, Sapna, there is the rural population there, and everything that happened was arranged in private homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 23 people, 23 Serbs, were killed in Rastosnica, according to this information here, and 15 more were captured and went missing. They were killed somewhere; in camps, prisons, who knows where. They were alive when they were taken away from Rastosnica, and their fate is unknown. They are still considered missing, although there is no possibility for them to be alive. You can see that there are women among them. The last one listed here, Dusanka Djokic, born in 1937, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't have this information, but further down in this document there is a list of persons responsible for the crimes that Mr. Ivanisevic was able to obtain, and in the last line again we see your name, "Asim Alic." Do you see that? It's in bold letters.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that among all the other names, only my name is bolded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's because --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness, regarding these two events, mentioned that Mr. Seselj said he was not there, he was not involved. He stated this very clearly. He knows nothing about all this, so I raise an objection because he's been repeating over and over the same question as to his involvement in these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, given this objection, you told us that you did not participate very well, this is what you're saying, but, remember, we have not been seized of this case. However, at the time, you were in charge of the police at Sapna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if the army captured prisoners and if these prisoners went through Sapna, you had to see them; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not bring them to the police station premises at all, so those who were brought, they were recorded, and I can talk about it. Everything else is just rumours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wanted to know the following: I want to know whether these people walked through the streets, you know, guarded by soldiers of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you do not deny the fact that the army, with its prisoners, passed through the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not denying that there were prisoners, but I don't know what happened to them, what was done to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, to save time, I'm not talking to the accused but to the counsel representing the accused. It happens to be the same person. There are two events, which according to you and according to this study, where Serbs were killed, and you even added that among the victims, there were civilians. To your knowledge, were there any legal follow-ups after these crimes? Did the competent judicial -- was the competent judicial authority seized? Were there any trials, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these places are still under Muslim control. They are part of the BH Federation, and to my knowledge no investigations have ever been carried out and no one has been prosecuted for the murder of Serbs in Rozanj and Rastosnica. You know that only the Serb accused are tried before the Tribunal, and there are just a couple of Croats, Muslims, or Albanians as a sort of objectivity. And if you see who is acquitted or sentenced to mild sentences, that's again Croats, Muslims and Albanians, while Serbs are sentenced to very harsh sentences, up to life sentence. So this really speaks nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, do you know where Baljkovica is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I duly noted what you have said, but the families of these victims may lodge a protest with the competent authority. I believe that in Sarajevo, there is a court in charge of this. Did they make a criminal complaint, was there a follow-up; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you ask really incredible questions. How should I know? I present the data obtained by this centre, headed by Mr. Ivanisevic, and he publishes his information. There are tens of thousands of testimonies by witnesses, victims, victims' family members, and as for who will prosecute whom, this is something that is really not my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you know that regarding the path of personal jurisdiction, Belgrade could very well be a competent authority, so if there are searches made, this could lead to something. This could have an impact on procedures, and this is what we are referring to. Were there any protests lodged or criminal reports lodged by the relatives of these missing persons in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madame Judge, Madame Judge, this question should have been asked to the Prosecution. If anyone should have this kind of information, it's them, not me. I never dealt with those topics before I came here to The Hague, and the Prosecution should know that. They should have an overview of all the crimes that happened against Serbs, against Muslims, against Croats, against Albanians, and so on. The Prosecution should have that, but their methods of selection are obviously very strange. They work in mysterious ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have -- it's you who brought the document where there is reference to this, so one could think that there was additional information in this document. But this document is just like any other. We will not take it into account, as such, but we will only take into account the witnesses [as interpreted] given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, to supplement what has just said and what my fellow Judge has just told you, you seem to put the blame on the fact that there has been no prosecution on the Prosecutor, himself. Maybe he did nothing. I don't know. I'm not in his office, I don't discuss with him, so I don't know anything about this. But if this Prosecutor here does nothing, if the prosecutor in Sarajevo does nothing, and if the prosecutor in Belgrade does nothing also, the families -- the relatives of these victims, as my fellow Judge just said, or this person who is heading an association dealing with the fate of Serbian victims, well, all these people can write to the Prosecutor and ask for some proceedings to be engaged. This is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right. Since this is being publicly broadcast, I think the victims will hear what you've just said and see what they can do about it. Mr. President, in Belgrade, quite by chance recently, one of the killers was arrested of the column of 200 soldiers who were leaving Tuzla, and I don't think the trial has started yet, but I think it is being prepared in Belgrade. And the West -- there's a great outcry in the West as to why Serbia's doing that, and there's a lot of pressure on them to have him returned to -- returned. And the High Representative Lajcak is even exerting pressure on Belgrade for this criminal to be set free. And now you're asking me about crimes in remote villages, for these matters might not have come out at all had not Mr. Ivanisevic not researched into them. So this is a crime against 200 soldiers who wanted to leave Tuzla, and they were killed in an ambush, and just one man was arrested because he was recognised as being a perpetrator. Now, there's enormous pressure exerted on Belgrade for him to be set free and returned to Tuzla. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You omitted to tell me, Mr. Alic, whether you know where Baljkovica is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You didn't allow me to answer that. I said I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the Judges didn't let you, not me.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Baljkovica and all these other places you mentioned earlier, I say with full responsibility here that the Serbs did return to those places, there was a return, and that they live there, and that your informers, the people who informed you, can ask them best, because they knew who did what.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, it doesn't say that you took part in the killing in this village, just for the previous two. That's what the witness statements say. But you must know what had gone on in those villages, because you were the top-ranking police official in Sapna, so that's why I'm asking you those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unless the credibility of the witness -- I don't know why we have all these questions about what's happening in this village in this case. If we're dealing with the credibility of the witness, fine, the accused can ask these questions, but it is becoming really tedious and repetitive. But I really don't see the relevance here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, these questions are based on two themes, either credibility or relevance. As far as relevance is concerned, this is not in the indictment, this is a backdrop and it's not challenged. Fine. So are you asking all these questions in order to test the credibility of this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They relate to both credibility of the witness and relevance, to both, and I think that the members of the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor have informed this witness sufficiently that he is believed on all counts and that I'm not believed at any time, so there's no point in commenting on that further. May I complete my cross-examination? And the witness seems to be completely relaxed today, compared to the state he was in yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber did not say that everything the witness is saying is true. Absolutely not. You are asking questions, and the Prosecutor raised to his feet to raise an objection. And I'm asking you the following question, because the objection was saying that you should stop your question, so I was asking you: What was the purpose of your question? You said, "Credibility." And I said, "Please continue." So don't say I'm preventing you from talking. I told you to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all these villages are in Zvornik Municipality, and it is my objective to show there were not only crimes on the Serb side, there were crimes on the Muslim sides as well, and that there was a bloody civil war going on in which many crimes were perpetrated. Now, the fact that The Hague Tribunal gives a false picture of this to the world, that it was the Serbs who were the main criminals in this war, that's something else, but I am showing that in all the localities mentioned in my indictment - I did this with Vukovar and Western Slavonia - that there were crimes on the other side, too, and sometimes far more crimes on the other side rather than on the Serb side. And we saw that with the example of Western Slavonia. So that is the crux of the matter and that's my right, that's my Defence case. So why are you interrupting me all the time? You warned me at least once that I was objecting too much while the Prosecutor was conducting his examination-in-chief. Now look at what's going on now, and you've never issued that caution to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, what's your objection? Before you take the floor, let me tell you that I am here in this function as Judge to assess the evidence, procedural problems, all these objections that seem to be a waste of time. All this seems to be completely unreasonable. We must assess the credibility of a witness, the relevance of what he is saying. Now, any Prosecutor can raise to his feet to challenging the Defence's case, just like the Defence can do exactly the same thing and raise endless objections, but in doing so, instead of looking at the merits of the case, you waste time -- we waste time in procedural matters. Each and everyone wanted to put forth his own opinion and his own point of view. We are here to render justice. It is not a justice -- justice in itself, not the justice of either of the parties. And all these procedural things are slowing things down. So you're going to raise another objection, and I assume it will be on the tu quoque. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I fully understand what you have said, Mr. President, but if I raise an objection, it is because there is something to object to. Paradoxically, my objection is trying to save time and not waste time on matters. The tu quoque, I'm not going to go into details on this, but we're not going to waste time on irrelevant issues. This is why I made an objection. These questions are not relevant. There's an armed conflict. What one party is doing doesn't justify what the other party is doing, and we are wasting time here, which is why I'm raising an objection. I believe we should move on to something that is more relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, to answer what you told us, you said earlier that in this conflict, not only the Serbs were involved, but the other parties also committed crimes. You said this. You mentioned two examples, gave us the examples of two villages. Fine, but please move on. You could list all the crimes which were committed in Bosnia-Herzegovina and we could spend hours on this. So please try and move forward. Please continue with this witness and move on. This witness could prove very useful to your case, possibly. If you want this witness to confirm crimes were committed, fine, I don't know, but ask him the question directly. And if he says, "Yes, there were crimes," then you can move on to something else. But it's always the same thing. You address a topic, the Prosecutor raises an objection, the Chamber must rule on the objection, and then you take the floor again, saying, "Look at this, the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution are hand in hand." You keep repeating this over and over again, but this is not true. This is not the way things work here. The Prosecutor rose to his feet several times, and you noted, through what he said and through what I said, that here we're trying to save time. So please, Mr. Seselj, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is correct that the crimes of one side cannot be justified by the crimes of the other side, because for each crime there is individual responsibility. However, in addition to the fact that the principle of collective responsibility for a crime has been introduced here, even national responsible for crimes, as far as I'm concerned, it is important for me to present, through the cross-examination, the general historical context of it all, because when somebody is held responsible for the crimes of one side, for example, if you have someone here who personally killed ten people and you're trying him, it is important for you the context in which he killed those people, the circumstances, whether some of his relatives had been killed, or people around him had been killed, or whether he killed just like that. That will -- the degree of criminal responsibility depends on that. So you can't prevent me from looking at the historical context of Zvornik in this case, and I'm just limiting myself to Zvornik. It was just a moment ago that I mentioned the killing of the 200 soldiers in Tuzla on the 15th of May, after which the Zvornik crimes happened, because almost all of them happened after the -- this date in May, the 15th of May, not before. So it was after the 15th of May that these atrocious crimes begin, and it is obvious that one of the reasons for those crimes being committed was the massacre of the column of soldiers who wanted to leave Tuzla. So please allow me to round this subject off. What can I do? I have my Defence case and the concept of my Defence case, and I insist upon it. I can't help it that time is running out. Now, you say here that the two parties are equal in the proceedings. In principle, that is true. The Defence and the Prosecution are, in principle, equal. However, if the Trial Chamber has to be biased and side with one party at a given moment, then it has to side with the accused and not with the Prosecutor. I assume you know that basic principle of law, and I'm just fighting here for the possibility of presenting my Defence case. It might be the worst Defence case and concept of a Defence case, but I know no better, so I'm doing my best, to the best of my ability. Now, the fact that the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution doesn't like the way I have conceived my Defence case, what can I do about that? Nothing. My Defence case is as I have conceived it, and I will bear the consequences of my Defence, so nobody should instruct me to defend myself in any way. Perhaps I'm doing it all wrong, but point a finger at any lawyer in this Tribunal who is conducting a Defence case better than I am conducting mine, and I will guarantee that you will find no such lawyer, there is no such person that does it better than me. May I be allowed to continue now, please, so that we can deal with this document before the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you may proceed. But in your explanation you gave us, an indication you could have told us in the first place. You just said that by proving that crimes were committed by the ABiH, this helps you lay the historical foundation to your case. Very well, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I hope you'll now be able to tell me, Mr. Alic, since you're so relaxed, where Baljkovica is.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well I didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you can't hear when you don't listen to anybody here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you're criticising me now, just like the Judges are criticising me and the Prosecutor, and now you are criticising me. So when you see a group of people in the street, as a policeman, people beating somebody who is innocent, instead of defending him, you get your baton out and start beating him too?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that's your observation, your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Go on, tell me again, where is Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Baljkovica is on the territory of the present municipality of Sapna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know that on the 9th of May, 1992, the Muslim Army attacked that village and killed 13 Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where Vitnica is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 20th of June, 1992, the Muslim Army attacked Vitnica and killed ten Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the Muslim Army cannot have attacked Vitnica when Vitnica is a village inhabited by Muslims. You don't assume they're going to attack themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many Serbs lived in that village?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not a single one, after these ten had been killed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs never lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how come they were killed, then, in that village?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Probably as the aggressors who attacked the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they were captured as aggressors and killed in the village?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There's just one thing that is certain, and it is this: They weren't killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There's one point that I'd like to make clear. The Serbs never inhabited Vitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, on the 20th of June, ten Serbs were killed there. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps in some attack on Vitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who attacked Vitnica then?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serbs attacked?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where Kamenica is, Gornja Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Zvornik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 24th of August, 1992, four Serb civilians were killed there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where Crni Vrh is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 10th of September, 1992, the Muslim Army organised an ambush, and they ambushed civilians, Serbs, in motor vehicles and killed seven people?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think that is the right information, because Crni Vrh was always under Serb control and the Muslims couldn't have set up an ambush there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the Muslims infiltrate a group there who killed civilians and then fled?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where Kocanje is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Kocanje?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where Novo Selo is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well it's mostly a Muslim village, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well Novo Selo has a hamlet, a Serb hamlet called Kocanje.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 17th of September there, seven Serb civilians were killed there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where Setici are?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 8th of October, 1992, eight Serb civilians were killed there, mostly women?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do know where Setici are -- where Setici is, and I know from that area a group of 700 or 800 Muslims were taken away by the Serbs, and no trace of them was ever found, not their graves, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 8th of October Cvijeta Pantic was born there, a woman born in 1910?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then we have Desa Pantic. She was born in 1924. Then we have Bosika Lukic, born in 1927, then Ljubica Pantic, another woman born in 1946, and Sava Pantic, she was born in 1920. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I assume somebody entered the cemetery and picked up these dates from the grave stones there, because you see, by those dates of birth, it seems absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you ashamed of the fact that the Muslim Army killed these old Serb women?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if that were true, I would be ashamed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
