utterances.text: Well, I'm ashamed, too, Mr. Alic, whenever I hear that the Serbs killed some Muslim civilians, for instance. And you, as the chief of police, must know about this event, whereas you claim that you don't and this is all invented?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The place you mentioned was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, and it is still on the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 8th of October, did a Muslim group of soldiers storm the place?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't know when the army stormed anything or when it launched operations, coordinated its work or anything like that. I didn't take part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Alic, you were aware of all the events in Zvornik Municipality. It is impossible that you didn't know about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I thought that you were going to ask me questions about October 1991 until the 8th of April, 1992, that period of time when I worked in Zvornik and lived in Zvornik, and when I had duties there. But you're asking me something that I have absolutely nothing to do with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were in Sapna, and Sapna was in Zvornik, too, until it was proclaimed a separate municipality, which was after the war; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where Malesici is located?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I've heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard that on the 8th of October, seven Serb locals were killed there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that, and I doubt that that information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know about Kamenica, Kamenica Donje?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 6th of November, at least 110 were killed there, and there are estimates that that figure could go as high as 250? They were killed with cold steel. These were prisoners. Only three of the prisoners were killed with firearms. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How can you not know when seven mass graves were exhumed on the 16th of February and the 15th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I haven't been following those events at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Registrar has just told me that you've had two hours. Your time is up, therefore. If you have one last question to put to the witness, put it to him, and then we will have the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have two and a half hours at my disposal, just as much as the Prosecution had. Please don't reduce my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've made a mistake. You have two and a half hours, but I would like the Registrar to confirm this. You have 30 minutes left. We will have a 20-minute break and resume. The Registrar needs to confirm this. You will have 30 minutes after that, and I hope there will be no further objections, and I hope that we can run through these 30 minutes without any objections. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, during the break did you check whether Zuco was interviewed as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe my colleague, Mr. Dutertre, could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I wanted to mention this, since we have resumed. The Tribunal has not interviewed Mr. Zuco -- Vuckovic. There is no ICTY statement of Vojin Vuckovic, but the Tribunal does have a series of documents, interviews and transcripts provided by the person in question to the local authorities. Some of these documents have been disclosed. Others have not. I am still conducting my search to see whether we have a comprehensive list. As things stand today, those documents that have not been disclosed yet will be disclosed very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Prosecutor has just told us that there has been no interview as a suspect of the person in question, but the Prosecution does have documents that have been provided by other legal authorities, other than the Tribunal. Some of these have been disclosed to you. Others have not been disclosed to you. They are currently drawing up a list, and this will be disclosed to you as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecution has disclosed to me Vojin Vuckovic, Zuco's, evidence at the Belgrade trial, where he testified in open session as the commander of the unit that comprised some of the accused. The Prosecution has also disclosed several documents related to the Sabac trial of Vojin Vuckovic, Zuco, and Dusan Vuckovic, aka, Repic, his brother. But if you look at the statement that Vojin Vuckovic gave yesterday, it says in the third paragraph: "The truth about my arrest, the arrest of my brother, Dusan, and Miroslav Bogdanovic and Semic Ulemek ..." It should read "Cema." That's Ulemek's first nickname. He was nicknamed "Legija" later on. I presented this truth on several occasions to the District Court in Sabac in 1993, the representatives of the OTP in Belgrade, in the presence of Defence counsel Dragoljub Djordjevic. So he says this lawyer was present. And then the Special Department for War Crimes of the District Court in Belgrade, the investigating judge for war crimes, Olimpic [phoen], and as a witness at the trial of the so-called Zvornik group in 2006 before the Trial Chamber with Judge Tatjana Vukovic presiding. I only received the last testimony and some documents relating to the Sabac trial. This interview with the representatives of the OTP, I don't know what the status of Mr. Vuckovic was, whether he was a witness or a suspect. That's not what I received, and I did not receive his statement given to the Investigating Judge. This has never been disclosed to me, and you can see that I did not receive the statement that Mr. Alic gave to the investigating judge in Sarajevo before his testimony at the Belgrade trial, and this would have been of interest to me, because the transcript of Mr. Alic's testimony in Belgrade shows that his statement to the investigating judge in Sarajevo was much more comprehensive than what he said in Belgrade in answer to the questions that were asked. That's what you can see from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the list provided by the Prosecution, make sure that you give as many documents as possible to Mr. Seselj. But there's one question you haven't answered. It seems that in 1993, in Belgrade, on the premises of the Belgrade tribunal, in the presence of a lawyer, the lawyer of the person in question, the OTP did have an interview, so this raises a question: Were there any notes? Is there an interview off the record, is there a record of this interview anywhere? And what was the status of this interview, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, we have not put -- questioned this person. In light of the new information provided by Mr. Seselj, I can conduct further researches. To the best of my knowledge today, I can say that I am not aware of an interview having been conducted by someone of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, one other point. You told us before the break that by putting your questions to the witness, you wanted to highlight the fact that crimes had been committed by people other than Serbs, and that this was part of your defence. The Trial Chamber would like to tell you, as regards this particular point, i.e., tu quoque, the elements that are part of the tu quoque are not assessed in terms of your responsibility. It's not because crimes were committed by others that you are exonerated from your own responsibility. This is what has been ruled by the Appeals Chamber, and this is -- remains constant. I would like to remind you of this. Personally, I feel that to shed some light on events which unfolded in a chronological order, you can, by way of information, put questions to the witness to highlight some factors which could explain people's behaviour, which could explain certain situations, and the aftermath to certain events. This is a possibility you have. This is, nonetheless, not tu quoque. You must make a distinction between tu quoque, which is a procedure likely to exonerate someone from his or her responsibility, from the information provided to a Chamber on circumstantial evidence, military, political situations, situations in the police, in the command of the army, and on the basis of these elements we can forge an opinion. Mr. Seselj, however, if, with the remaining time you have left, you only want to do tu quoque, then it's at your own risk, because you are then wasting time. In its discretion, the Trial Chamber can shorten the cross-examination of a witness if it feels that it is not relevant and if it feels that it is wasting time. I'm telling you this because I would like to understand what it is you want to demonstrate to us. I think it would be wise for you to give us some information beforehand. This would mean that the Prosecution would not get to his feet all the time. So it might be a good idea if you could tell us beforehand, "With such-and-such a witness, I will address such-and-such a factor and I will emphasise such-and-such an element," and then maybe we will be able to better understand your strategy. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Seselj be kind enough to tell me when, in 1993, an ICTY investigator was present, since the ICTY was created in mid-1993. This means I could streamline my research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if you have any information about this meeting which took place in Belgrade between the OTP and Zuco, could you give us the date, unless you don't know the date, which is perfectly understandable, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is no date for this interview, just information that this was done in the presence of a lawyer, Dragoljub Djordjevic. And you mentioned -- and you made a mistake when you mentioned 1993, because the 1993, that's the year when the trial before the District Court in Sabac took place, and that's what it says in the document. And now the Prosecutor is sticking to this date, 1993. I think that the best thing to do, because there have been so many problems about statements that have not been disclosed to me, for instance, the statement by General Zivota Panic and Aleksandar Vasiljevic, I think that the best course of action would be for the Prosecution to provide me with a list of all the statements it took from persons in the capacity of suspects and from all persons who were interviewed as potential witnesses, and then I could go through all those names and their basic personal details and decide what might have something to do with the indictment issued against me and what might not. I think that would be a good solution, but I'm not optimistic enough to expect that this would, in fact, happen. Regarding this caution that you've just given me, I am prepared to -- everything, I'm prepared that you would not only reduce my time for cross-examination, but that you would prevent me from cross-examining at all. You are asking me to indicate what my cross-examination would be based on, and why is it that nobody explains to me, the Prosecution or the Judges, this is the 20th witness to appear here, what has the Prosecution managed to gain, to corroborate, the charges in the indictment through the testimony of the 20 witnesses? Perhaps I am the stupidest person here because I don't see it, but I fail to see what the Prosecution has proven about my guilt. And we have heard 20 witnesses here. Where is my guilt? You are attacking me because of my Defence case, and I'm completely relaxed because I can see any -- I cannot see any shred of guilt that has been proven through the testimony of all those witnesses. And now it is my fault that I'm wasting time. I'm wasting only the time that you have given me, and I am entitled to decide how I want to spend this time, whether I should devote it to challenge the credibility of the witness, or casting a light on relevant events, or on explaining the historical context. I have full freedom to decide on that, and I don't have to explain to anyone why it is that I decided this. Historical context is important for each and every trial. The fact that I am not exonerated from my guilt by the fact that other people committed crimes, this is not relevant for me, because I can't see what is the crime that I committed so that I could say, "Oh, well, somebody else did that, and you can see he got away with it, and I am here." Perhaps you are aware of that, but I am not, and that is why my Defence case is as it is. If you want to take my time away from me, that's up to you. You cannot spring any surprises on me. I've been through lots of things in these six years, and nothing can surprise me. And I am not tense in any way. I am prepared for every option. And to tell you the truth, the best thing for me would be the worst option. That's the one that I'm really ready to tackle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody wishes to take your time away from you. You have the same time as the Prosecution. That is not the issue, but the Trial Chamber is here to make sure that the rights of the Defence are respected. And we could actually point out to you a Defence strategy that may seem suicidal. If you do tu quoque all the time, this will have no impact whatsoever on the facts to be considered by the Bench. This is what I wanted to tell you. As far as the historical context is concerned, of course you can highlight this, but don't spend the best part of your time discussing the historical context, since we have been seized of the indictment, with paragraph 6 of the indictment with joint criminal enterprise, and the list of crimes and your responsibility therein listed in paragraphs 7, 8 and 9 of the indictment, and paragraph 10 also; i.e., the way in which you participated in the joint criminal enterprise in a number of acts. So you could purposefully reread these paragraphs. Contrary to what you may believe, and this is something which I wanted to tell you, I was waiting for the right time and now I have an opportunity to discuss this with you now, as far as the Yellow Wasps are concerned and the volunteers of the SRS, of course, if it is established that those people who committed the crimes were not people whom you sent out in the field to commit these crimes, this may be a problem. But as far as -- or in terms of the case law of this Tribunal and the submissions of the Prosecutor, you are held liable for the crimes, including the crimes committed by the Yellow Wasps and the White Bees, who were not under your control. This is how one can read the indictment. So I beseech you to reread these paragraphs of the indictment so that you do not omit this. You have 30 minutes left to cross-examine this witness. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as I'm concerned, I would not be surprised if I were to be charged with the murder of John Kennedy. Well, they could put that in the indictment with the same arguments that they used for all the other charges. I am not concerned about the joint criminal enterprise charges, because it's always the Serbs who are responsible for that. Serbs are criminals because they oppose the world powers, the European Union, Great Britain, the United States. That's why we're criminals. And we oppose them because we stand for universal justice, and might is in the hands of injustice. This Tribunal is in the hands of injustice, and that is my approach to this trial. As my own Defence counsel, I am entitled to have a specific philosophical approach to my Defence. There is no need for me to be cautioned by you, because I understand everything. I am completely aware about the background of this trial, and I can't see why you keep expressing your dissatisfaction with the way that I'm proceeding with my Defence case. It's no skin off your teeth. I decided what is the best way to do it, and I am sticking by my concept, and I'm quite successful, I have been successful so far. I tore down practically all of the witnesses, I razed them to the ground, including three major experts. If you think that I haven't been successful, well, you can deliver the judgement. You can just mail the judgement to me, I don't have to come here, because this is really -- I'm being really mistreated during the transportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, your statement of principle which you have just exposed to us is nothing new. You have already mentioned this, so just please resume your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you were shown this document yesterday. That's the statement by Vojin Vuckovic, aka Zuco. So to save some time, let us move on to paragraph 4 in the statement. In the first paragraph, he presents his personal details. In the second, he gives the general view of your testimony. We talked about it yesterday. I hope that I managed to use the third paragraph -- that I discussed it with the Prosecution and the Judges, not wasting my time. In paragraph 4, he says: "Claims that Asim Alic made on several occasions that he questioned four capture Serbs until late in the afternoon, I being one of them, are notorious lies, because all the interrogations ended by 8.15 a.m., and after that we were subjected to horrible torture and physical abuse, injuries that were inflicted on us were visible with the naked eye, and they were inflicted by rifle-butts." Is what Mr. Vuckovic is saying true?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Alic, Mr. Vuckovic says here -- well, I'm referring to both you, using the title "Mr." As a courtesy. The fourth man listed here, he identifies him as Miroslav Bogdanovic. In your statements of 1996 and 1997, you spoke about Stojanovic, and then at your testimony at the Belgrade trial, you mention Zvezdan Jovanovic, and here again in your examination-in-chief, you said the fourth one was Zvezdan Jovanovic, and you knew full well that this was a man who was accused of murdering Djindjic. I think this was a false accusation. Had it been the case, he would hold the same place in the Hall of Fame of the Serb people as Gavrilo Princip. But I wanted to ask you, why did you use the name Zvezdan Jovanovic, for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you, is this the man that we were talking about yesterday, one of the Vuckovic brothers that you said was a psychopath, mentally deranged? Is that the one you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you, Mr. Alic, should know about that. Let's not play like little kids. The guy who was a psychopath, he hanged himself in prison. This Vojin Vuckovic, aka, Zuco, the commander of the volunteer detachment, Igor Markovic, which was part of the Zvornik Territorial Defence, and that unit was later renamed Yellow Wasps. At first it was part of the Territorial Defence, and then it became a renegade unit. You know that full well.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Whose Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence of the Serb municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, how could they be in the Serb municipality of Zvornik when they came from Serbia and the surrounding parts of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's easy. They relocate to Zvornik, and there you have it. And you saw yesterday a document from the Serb police, that it was in fact a unit that rallied 80 locals from Zvornik and just 20 from Serbia. That's a document dating to 1992. But don't ask questions of me, you answer my questions, and my question is: Why did you use the name of Zvezdan Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, avoid putting questions to the accused, please, because it is for the accused to put questions to you. This is part of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Yes. On that day when we had people arrested in the police station, from their ID cards, the ones they had on them -- well, that's what it said in their ID cards. I could not, with certainty, remember all the names, but judging by the descriptions given by the citizens who were in the camps, who were in the camps, as I said, I came to the conclusion that it was those people, because that's how they called them -- or, rather, they called each other -- they addressed each other that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, not a single victim witness mentions anyone by the name of Zvezdan.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You didn't talk to the victims. I took statements from the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But many of those statements have been disclosed to me here, and Zvezdan is mentioned nowhere. So you invented the mention of Zvezdan?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Many of those statements are to be found in the Cantonal Prosecutor's Office at Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I assume the OTP should have disclosed that to us on time so we could see how Mr. Alic invented that. I'm now going to read a more lengthy paragraph, where Mr. Vuckovic goes on to explain the situation over the arrest of these four men, and he says: "We were arrested in the night between the 7th and 8th of April, 1992, at 1.00 a.m. at the entrance to Zvornik by a hamlet called Mekarica [phoen]. We were stopped there by a group of some 20 Muslims, without any markings or insignia, with no uniforms, armed with automatic weapons of Hungarian manufacture, so-called Kalashnikovs. In that group, there was Zvornik criminals organised by Asim Alic, and they were Siman Karamaric [phoen] and the brothers Mustafa and Benjamin Halilovic. We were then tied up and taken at knife-point to the fire brigade in Zvornik, where the Crisis Staff was located for the Party of Democratic Action, which was controlled by Asim Alic, with members of the OUP, that is to say, the police, which was made up of Muslims exclusively. Between 2.30 hours and 4.15 hours, we were at the fire brigade building when Asim Alic arrived and took us prisoners off to the police station in Zvornik. In the morning hours, somewhere at around 7.00 a.m., from the discussion between Asim Alic and Fadil Mujic, we heard their conversation. In front of the police station, there were over --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd actually like to know what the question is. There's so many questions, if the question comes at the end, it will obviously be a compounded question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Seselj will put a question after having read what Zuco tells about the circumstances in which he was arrested and detained, so let him finish reading the paragraph, since we don't have a translation of this document. Please continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In front of the station, there were over 300 Muslims extremists who demanded the leadership of MUP to take us outside so that they could drink the blood of young Serbs. Then Fadil Mujic took over responsibility for us prisoners and took us to his office on the second floor. He took the handcuffs off us, locked the door, and said, 'Don't make any trouble for me. I'll do everything in my power to prevent the worst from happening and to see that you're returned home and that no blood is shed, as many of those present in the police station would like to see. I'll try and effect an exchange.' Fadil Mujic was the only man who came to visit us during the conflict on the 8th of April 1992. At around 1830 hours, he took us out of the police station in Zvornik, towards Divic, and handed us over to the border units of the JNA Army at the hydro electric power plant at Mali Zvornik. He was assisted by Mustafa Zekic, and I, to pay him back, put his family up in my house at Umka, where he stayed until the end of the war. Mustafa Zakic is a driving instructor in Austria, and I have contact with him over the phone." Do you know Mustafa Zakic.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is what Mr. Vuckovic says here true?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: None of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... compound question. There's so many information in this question, I've already said this earlier, it's totally impossible to ask a question in such a fashion, read a paragraph for five minutes and then say whether it's the truth. You have to refer to the first sentence, second sentence, third sentence. This is not an appropriate way of asking questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you have heard the objection raised by the Prosecutor. I don't personally share his opinion, with a witness who is not here and who made this statement, this document. So please try and put short questions in order to highlight what you would want to highlight for your case. We talked about Mustafa Jakic, so please proceed. Otherwise, the Prosecutor will say there were so many elements in your question that we will not know where to start. So please proceed step by step.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am conscious of the fact that it is the Prosecution's aim for me to lose as much time as possible and not to be able to complete an analysis of Mr. Vuckovic's statement, so I give up on the previous question and am going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, do you know where the village of Rastosnica is located?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's in the area of the Zvornik Municipality; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and I answered that in my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Milan Petrovic, who was a tradesman in Rastosnica?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Was his nickname Pusula?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Then I've heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know he was trafficking in weapons?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that he was selling weapons to both the Serbs and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what the price of a Kalashnikov was, how much he was selling Kalashnikovs for?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't want to make guesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Shall I remind you? Was it around 500 Deutsche marks or more expensive than that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was more expensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Around a thousand marks, would you say?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thereabouts, even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: More; right. Now, it's very important for me that you were able to identify that man and say you knew him. Now we'll see from the next paragraph on page 2 what Dusan Vuckovic says about the reasons for their arrival in Zvornik: "I, my brother, Dusan Vuckovic, Miroslav Bogdanovic and Semic Ulemek," and it should say "Cema Ulemek there," that was Ulemek's nickname at the time, "Came into Zvornik at our own initiative on the 4th of April 1992 in order to take -- because of the investigation that Bogdanovic and Semic were conducting because of weapons sales, long-barrel and short-barrel rifles conducted by self-appointed colonel Pusula from a place called Rastosnica, near Zvornik, both with the Serbs and with the Muslims. We announced our arrival for the 7th of April, 1992, and the leadership of the SDS, and they were supposed to tell us where Pusula was located. I arrived in Zvornik as personal security detail for Miroslav Bogdanovic, who worked for the Military Security Service, and my brother was with us just by chance." Now, my question for you is this: Did you know that this man, Pusula, was a self-appointed colonel?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know that he had a group of armed people as an escort, that he moved around with this group of people?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did know that he engaged in trafficking. He had his own buses driving from Belgrade to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, I reminded you of the fact that Fadil Mujic, in the Belgrade trial, said, and we have this in the transcript, that he -- that Colonel Boskovic personally from Belgrade intervened because of these four men who had been arrested. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. Fadil said that, so he is the one who can confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I hope we are going to hear Fadil Mujic in the courtroom as well in due course. Now, does this coincide with what Mr. Vuckovic says, and does it coincide with what we heard from Fadil Mujic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it doesn't coincide, because Vuckovic -- well, I'm thinking along these lines: I don't think they were authorised or capacitated to conduct any investigations in the territory of another state, where the official police force was in existence, a legal police force. I think that's absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, is it obvious to you that the Military Security Service here had no other way of getting to self-appointed Colonel Pusula, because we're dealing with the first days of April here? Was there anyone else who could have arrested him there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Since Pusula was a civilian, it came under our authority and we should have done that, if that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, why, when you learned that Pusula was trafficking in weapons, did you not arrest him straight away?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He wasn't at his residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was at his village all the time, but it didn't enter your mind to entering that village because you were afraid of entering that village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were afraid of no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, why did you flee, then, on the 8th of April, why did you take to your legs so fast?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because we were shelled with grenades, we were shelled, and there were tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But this man says that nobody -- that the -- there were certain targets, but there were no victims as a result of the firing?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Mujic said, and I don't want to comment on his statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is all right. Mr. Vuckovic goes on to say in paragraph 2 on page 2 the following; that you lied when you claimed that he had long hair. He always had short hair and a receding hairline, and he said: "He recognised me in a lineup under number 8, and on it you can see that my hair is short." So Zuco claims he never had long hair, whereas in examination-in-chief you said he had long hair, too?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's what he looked like at the time. He could have cut his hair the very next day, couldn't he, and then it would have been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How could he have cut his hair when he was in your hands?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, on the 8th of April, towards -- in the afternoon, he was under our control, but already in the evening he was in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, I see. Let's move on to paragraph 3. Mr. Vuckovic says as follows: "As far as the identification cards are concerned which were allegedly found on us, the truth of the matter is that I had an ID card of the Serbian Chetnik Movement issued on the 12th of June, 1991, for that year." And he reminded me of something here that I had forgotten. When the Serbian Chetnik Movement existed and the ID was issued only within 1991, they were ID cards issued for only one year, and, Judges, from the piece of evidence that the Prosecutor supplied, with the list of the ID cards, it said for the year, and the year entered there was "1991," as far as I remember. So the IDs of the Serbian Chetnik Movement were issued for just one year, they were valid for just one year. And then he goes on to say the following: "I left the Serbian Chetnik Movement officially on the 3rd of September, 1991. The other card that Alic mentions is one that I received from Zjelko Raznjatovic, Arkan, in October 1991, when I handed over the family weapons belonging to Mirko Livadinovic from the Serbian Volunteer guard who was killed in Rostovo, and it related to fuel taken at his petrol pump in Belgrade." Do you remember any ID card on the -- or, rather, any card on the basis of which you could tank up with fuel at Arkan's petrol pump in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the text is being read paragraph by paragraph. Afterward, whether this is tendered into evidence or not, it will end up being in the -- on the record, it will be in the file, because it will be on the transcript. I believe that Rules 92 ter, 92 quater and 92 bis are bypassed here, because he is reading everything. In the Rule, there are a number of conditions, a number of criteria, that are not met here. Mr. Seselj is doing exactly the same as he was doing yesterday, he is reading verbatim documents, and normally there are specific rules to tender these documents. He's not asking formally for these documents to be tendered into evidence, but they end up being on the transcript. And because of that, they end up being on the record and in evidence. This is why I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's on the transcript. Mr. Seselj, I'm sure that you have taken due note of what the Prosecutor has said. Would you like to answer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think this is intentionally time being wasted by the Prosecutor, because, Judge, on several occasions you said that you were interested in the -- in hearing the answers of the witness to my questions. Now, what I'm going to base my questions on, well, I have to base them on something every time, or I'll say, "Somebody told me or somebody phoned me up and said ... ," or I'm going to show a document, a piece of paper. This is a bit more convincing rather than me saying to Mr. Alic, "I heard such-and-such had taken place." At least I think so. Now, you can do what you will. I have to ask questions based on something, because the witness has the advantage. He was a participant in all the events, whereas I was far away from these events. So how can I tackle the problem unless I talk to people and gather information? And the Prosecutor is intentionally wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Furthermore, Mr. Vuckovic goes on to say the following: "I wish to stress that I was never a member of the Serbian Radical Party." And if I tell you that nowhere in the records of the Serbian Radical Party will you find the name of Mr. Vuckovic, this particular Dusan Vuckovic with this CV, what can you say to that, Mr. Alic, what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't keep your records and the records of your membership. This person said himself that he had an ID and confirmed what I asserted, the ID of the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I didn't challenge that, either. He probably had that. He could have had it. Now, he goes on to say here of what parties he was a member after 1998, and not to make those parties angry and it's not relevant, I won't mention them. But he goes on to say: "I put forward this information because I wish to explain that Professor Dr. Vojislav Seselj had no points in common with the unit that I was in command of, nor did that unit have anything at all to do with the Serbian Chetnik Movement or the Serbian Radical Party." What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have no comment to make there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Now, he mentions the killing of Serbian taxi driver that you mention in your statement as well. You say there that it was never established who killed this Serbian taxi driver, isn't that right, and the Serbs claim that he was killed by a Muslim, by Muslims, and the Muslims claim that it was the Serbs who killed him, to throw the onus on the Muslims, and the taxi driver's throat was slit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's what my information says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vuckovic goes on to say the brutal killing of the taxi driver, whose name was Sasa, the Muslims recorded on videotape because they had to substantiate their loyalty to the Muslim authorities in that way: "Asim Alic was duty-bound to send on the tape to the Federal Ministry of the Interior." Now, did you ever have that tape in your hands, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. This event had already happened before I moved from Belgrade to Zvornik, to work in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not accusing you of -- I'm not accusing you of you having killed anyone or having persuaded anyone to kill anyone, but have you heard of the existence of that tape?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, never. Now, who could at that time have recorded all this on videotape without being identified?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now he goes on to speak about the killing of the JNA warrant officer in Sapna and the investigation conducted by the JNA investigative authorities, and I don't want to dwell on that, but just to say that he claims that all the information is today to be found in the Military Security archives and that the documents have not been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. Earlier, you addressed the issue of the ID cards, and then you moved on to something else, but this is extremely important as far as the credibility of this witness is concerned. Witness, let's go back a little. We have a witness of a person that is not here in front of us, but who made a formal statement, a written statement. I asked Mr. Seselj yesterday whether, by law, when you make a formal written statement, you could be prosecuted for false testimony, yes, and the one who is using it could be charged with being an accomplice also. But this being said, the outcome of what Mr. Seselj read and to which Mr. Prosecutor objected, that this person was arrested under a number of conditions, and that this person had two IDs. The first ID card was for the Chetnik Movement and had been delivered in 1991, issued in 1991. Mr. Seselj highlighted that there are years mentioned in these -- on these cards. Zvornik happened in 1992, so theoretically you should have had a card by the Chetnik Movement dated 1992. The Serbian Radical Party happened to have been created on February 23rd, 1991, and because of this, he could have had a card also from the Serbian Radical Party. But the problem, what you're saying, is that according to Mr. Seselj, this person was not a member of the Serbian Radical Party. They had to check the lists. Furthermore, the second ID card, as it exists and as is not contested by Zuco, is an ID card that was handed over and issued by Arkan, which has nothing to do with the ID card of the Serbian Radical Party, unless Arkan would be an agent of the Serbian Radical Party. It seems that there is something that does not -- that doesn't correspond to the written statement that we have, the written statement of this Zuco witness who testified in writing. Maybe he's lying, I don't know, but this is one element, and I must assess this element. I can't just set it aside and say it's of no interest. This would not be professional. As a professional judge, I must assess all the elements and all the elements that are brought up during the cross-examination. To sum up, the witness says there are two ID cards, one from the Chetnik Movement and the second one is a card that was issued by Arkan. Secondly, the Serbian Radical Party, according to its president, who is here with us in this courtroom, says that this person was not a member of the Serbian Radical Party at the time. Are you absolutely, 100 per cent sure of having seen a card of the Serbian Radical Party in the hands of these people that you arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not expect this gentleman to tell the truth. It is in his interests to lie. It is not in my interests to lie. I have come here. I was summoned by you to tell the truth, and nothing else. What I have said, I'm still maintaining. I still stick by what I have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's proceed with the cross-examination. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that in the meantime, we have received the translation in French and English of the passage that you asked to be translated yesterday. I don't know if you want to go into this. I just obtained this translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, and, Mr. Registrar, I'd like to know how much time Mr. Seselj has. I believe time is almost up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have ten minutes left, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you say that it is not in your interests to lie, but on the 10th of May, 2006, when you testified in Belgrade, you were caught in a lie at page 41 and page 42 of the transcript, and you refused to answer the questions that pertained to the contradictions. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was instructed there that I need not respond to questions that I was not sure about or any questions that might incriminate me or discredit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, fine, Mr. Alic. I'm not going to ask you any questions that might discredit you or compromise you.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You can't do that, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I think you're mistaken there, but I have also testimony from Dusan Vuckovic, Zuco, at the Belgrade trial, the 16th of December. This was disclosed to me by the Prosecution. At page 5 and at page 7 of transcripts of his testimony, he again mentions Colonel Nedzo Boskovic as he was then, and the task to capture Busal [phoen] and the fact that Nedzo Boskovic intervened by phone called the Zvornik police station to secure the release of the four arrested persons. The Prosecution can check that at pages 5 and 7 of the Belgrade transcripts, since I'm running out of time. Mr. Vuckovic goes on to say, about how the video recording that we watched here was made up, but I'm not going to go into that. I would like to move on to document number 6. That's a statement by Colonel Radomir Tacic. He says here that he followed the -- my trial and that he was outraged by the lies presented by Witness Asim Alic, and that he wanted to clear up some things about areas where my name was mentioned. You can see that Colonel Tacic says: "I claim --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, obviously here the accused is just reading documents without putting any questions, and this is not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, on several occasions I explained things to you, but I think you find it hard to understand. In order to ask questions, he must first lay the foundations for the questions. Some statements are handed to him. Colonel Tacic, who we already mentioned yesterday. I note that this trial is closely monitored, because we have spontaneous witnesses that spring up and make spontaneous statements, just like this colonel who has just sent a document to the Defence. I do not know what is included in this document because it's written in Serbian. So in order to try and understand the document, we have to have the passages read to us. So he must absolutely read those passages and put the question. He can't ask the question without us knowing what the contents of this document is. Just put yourself in our shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just talking -- [In English] " ... recording that we watch here was made up, but I'm not going into that." [Interpretation] So he's talking about things, he's reading the statement, actually, he's not putting any question, and this is not an appropriate way of cross-examining a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe this escaped me because things are going extremely fast. Obviously, you've read a passage and forgot to ask a question. Maybe you didn't ask a question after what you've read. So, please, read a passage, but then ask a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not true, Mr. President. In one sentence, I explained why I didn't want to read the passage, because it concerned a video recording, and I didn't have time. If I had time, I would deal with that. Mr. Vuckovic explains how the video recording was made, the recording that was shown here in court, the recording where we hear him say a couple of words. We saw it in examination-in-chief. I don't want to waste my ten minutes on this. Other things are more important to me. And I just briefly explained why I wanted to skip that, and the Prosecution wants me to waste as much time as possible. May I continue? I do hope that I still have my ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tacic says, relating to what you said in your statement and repeated here, how you escorted him to Zvornik and attended the meeting at the police station: "I claim that I never met Mr. Alic. The first time that I saw him was on TV, while he testified in the trial of Professor Dr. Vojislav Seselj. At the time that Mr. Asim Alic testified about, I was the chief of staff of the 4th Armoured Brigade, and in this capacity I talked with representatives of Serbs and representatives of the Muslims in the territory of the municipality of Zvornik. The civilian police never helped me pass through any roadblocks. I did not ask for any such assistance, nor did I need it. Alic is lying through his teeth when he says that he knew me, that he would give me a lift and take me across the roadblocks. Throughout my stay in the area, I had my personal driver, whose name was Radinko Matic. I repeat, once again, I claim that apart from my driver, Matic, I was never driven by anyone else during my stay in Zvornik. I give this statement voluntarily under no duress, and I agree that Professor Dr. Vojislav Seselj used this in the trial before the Tribunal in The Hague." So what do you say to that? This is completely contrary to what you said in your statement in 1996 and in your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can say the following: I didn't drive Colonel Tacic, I followed him in my police car. I was ordered by my chief to wait for him just before the roadblock that was located at the factory. I couldn't go there. I didn't even approach that area, because I couldn't do that. Colonel Tacic passed through that roadblock in his own car, and I was waiting there for him, and I followed him in the official police car to the municipality building. After the meeting was over, I again escorted him or followed him from the municipality building to the area where he had come from, but I did not approach the roadblock was that posed a danger to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, in your statement, you said that you, yourself, attended the meeting, and he claims that you did not. And you talked about the contents of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's not what I said. The meeting was held at the municipality building. My chief, the chief of the Public Security Station, was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you said that, yourself, was present there.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me find this. I will find that, Mr. Alic, even if I have to spend all my remaining time for that. That's your statement, the 1997 statement, page 5. It says here that you went to an area just in front of the roadblock to receive Colonel Tacic, and then you say: "When I followed Colonel Tacic back to the police station in Zvornik, he had a meeting with my chief, and I was present there." Now we go on to page 6: "During the meeting, Colonel Tacic told us that he had information that 5.000 members of the Green Berets were in Zvornik and that he had 70 tanks in Celopek. He threatened that Zvornik would come under an attack if we did not cooperate with him. Nothing was agreed at the meeting, so I escorted Colonel Tacic to the same location where I had picked him up." So when did you lie, when you gave the statement or here in the courtroom, because you had to have lied at one point?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I am not telling any lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are there any such people?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not lie in the courtroom, I did not lie before. I said that I escorted him to the municipality building and that a meeting with the political leaders was held there, attended by Osman Mustafic, chief of the Public Security Station, and that later on Mustafic had a meeting with us and he told us what had happened at the previous meeting. And after that, I again escorted Colonel Tacic in an official car to the roadblock, and the same thing that I'm saying now, I said the first time. And earlier, I don't know what the interpretation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you signed it with your own hand in 1996, 1997. There were still some honest people in the Prosecution. You signed this in your own hand. You did not make any corrections. I caught you lying again.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't lie at all. There may be an error in translation. I made the same statement then and I make the same statement now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm sure that you managed to convince the Judges and the Prosecution that you did not tell a lie, but the public is also following this, and I am relying on the public. Mr. Alic, let us go on. You heard about Milivoj Dukic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know who that man is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How can that be, Mr. Alic? He was a colleague of yours in the police brigade in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I can't let this be said. This is insulting for the Judges, and I shall tell you why. You've just said, concerning what the witness might have said, that what he's saying, well, the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber believe what he has said. You anticipate the assessment we are going to make, and you are saying this publicly. And I would like to state publicly that this does not work, and this is a very serious matter. It's a travesty of the truth that you are presenting us with. The witness makes statements, written statements, the witness testifies. You show a document which could establish that this does not coincide with what Mr. Tacic has said. Very well. We will see afterwards what conclusions we need to draw, but you are anticipating conclusions and you are saying that these are the same as the findings of the Prosecution. And this is not right, and I wish to tell you so publicly. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if that is insulting for the Judges, then I withdraw that part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has withdrawn this, so no more will be said about it. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution also objects to that part of the accused's statement, where he indicates he's relying on the public. It's unclear. Relying on the public to do what? But again we raise issues concerning intimidation to future witnesses, and that statement could be perceived by members of the public in that light, and we would put that object on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you have withdrawn what you have just said, and this has been noted. But once again, the Bench is totally independent from the Prosecution. The Prosecution is like you. The OTP presents its case, you present your case, and the Bench will assess it. This is how it works. You may have a different opinion about this, but this is how it works, and the Trial Chamber has demonstrated many a time that we did not agree with the OTP at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I hope that you and your colleagues, because of your anger to my words, did not fail to hear what Mr. Mundis has just said. Mr. Mundis is wondering what public it is that I'm counting on, but he is forgetting that the principle of the public character in a criminal trial is the most important principle, that without this principle of the public counting on the trial can you have a regular trial. And, secondly, how is it that he thinks that I'm instilling fear into future witnesses by cross-examining present witnesses? I assume that any witness that appears in this courtroom knows in advance that he has to face a monster here that is going to completely refute his testimony, and all the other lawyers appearing before the Tribunal ought to behave the same way. They wouldn't try and make up to the Prosecutor, but they would be governed by the rules of cross-examination applied in the Anglo-Saxon legal system. So the witness must be aware that he will be subject to cross-examination and challenging of his credibility and reliability, and that if he has something to hide, I will find it out. If there's anything that can compromise him, I will find it out and present it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the fact that the proceedings are public is one thing, but when we are talking about -- when we are talking about legal proceedings, but you told us yourself this morning that you were speaking to the public, and not because this was part of legal proceedings. Do you remember having said that this morning? You said you were particularly keen on making sure that the public at large would know that crimes had been committed and the Serbs fell victims to these crimes committed by Croats and Muslims, and you clearly said this. This was intended for the public, but these are legal proceedings, and both parties take the floor and make their submissions so that the Bench can draw its own conclusions on the allegations put forward. And as regards your alleged responsibility, we are not talking to the public at large. What we are interested in are the legal proceedings. This is not a political platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, with all due respect, I want to make the objection that I raised or the point that I raised absolutely clear. I'm not necessarily at this point talking about the public versus non-public nature of what's happening in this courtroom. I completely agree and the Prosecution completely agrees with the notion that trials must be open to the maximum extent possible. What I'm objected to is reflected on lines 14 through 16 of page 77, where there's a reference to Dr. Seselj relying on the public. In the context of what he said, and I think it should be repeated, he said: "I'm sure that you managed to convince the Judges and the Prosecution that you did not tell a lie, but the public is also following this, and I am relying on the public." And to the extent that might have certain implications, we put on the record our objection that that could cause intimidation of this or other witnesses whom this accused has asserted are less than truthful. A public statement that he will rely on the public with respect to what he calls false witnesses or witnesses who are less than truthful is a point to which we will object and place that objection on the record, and I want to make it very clear that that's what we're objecting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Mundis. Your concern is now on the record. Mr. Seselj, would you like to take the floor again. And finish your cross-examination, because you have two minutes, maximum, left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to react to what Mr. Mundis said first and to what Judge Lattanzi said as well. I have to rely on the public, because I don't have anybody else to rely upon, and it is my right to rely upon the public, and the public nature of these proceedings is guaranteed precisely so that I can rely on public opinion, because you're trying me but the public is trying you, Judges, and that's why I rely upon the public, and that's why the public is very important, as far as I'm concerned, very important to me, so that I'm not just at your beck and call and your will, I don't rely on your will, because if I depended on that, I wouldn't defend myself at all, I absolutely would not. But as the public is a mighty defender of me, not only the Serb public but the international public as well because many legal circles are attending this trial with great attention, I feel far better than I would if you were to try me somewhere else in the dark. Now, what Mr. Mundis has just said, that my statements and relying on the public represents intimidation of future witnesses, well, that's just nonsensical, that's ludicrous. That I'm intimidating a future witness? I am, by telling him that if he lies, I'm going to dispel those lies in the courtroom, I'm going to uncover them, and this is because the Prosecution has had an easy job of it in other trials, where lies were just put out and the Defence counsel didn't even try to find them out, because witnesses have a hard time here, whereas in other trials they were sovereign in presenting their testimony. But after me, the witnesses totter out of the courtroom. One got lost going to the toilet. Many things happen in this courtroom. And now you want me not to rely on the public. Who am I to rely on, if it is not the public, because the voice of the public is God's voice, as far as I am concerned, because it is that public that will make the final judgement, both of me and of all the rest of you who are taking part in this trial, and you have to count on that. Perhaps Mr. Mundis comes from a system where the philosophy of law is not taught, whereas in the European system the philosophy of law is one of the most important subjects taught at the Faculty of Law. Without the philosophy of law, Mr. Mundis, you can't embark upon any serious trial. If did you just think it's enough to collect witness statements and an enormous amount of documents and that is enough. Why don't you take a look around you, and you'll see that the Prosecutor never conducted any kind of investigation, no investigation at all. All it does is collect up witness statements, many of which are contradictory amongst themselves, you bring in a witness to testify one way, another in another one and another in a third way, and they are all Prosecution witnesses. So why did you not conduct an investigation? It's investigations exist in continental law and in the Anglo-Saxon type of law, and the Prosecution, the OTP of this Tribunal is conducting no investigation, there isn't any kind of investigation. It's just a hodge-podge of different statements and heaps of documents, 90 per cent of which are irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In these proceedings, on the fact that these are made public, we know that they are public, and that is not called into question. You have explained to us that you were cross-examining the witnesses and this was intended for the public. That's your problem. But as far as the Judges are concerned, and my colleague has told you this also, the cross-examination must unfold as part of the legal proceedings, because this is what will be assessed at the end of the trial in an adversarial system, where we have the Prosecution, the witness and the Defence. The public is one thing; the legal proceedings are another. You have told us that for you it's all the same. That's your position. You are free to think what you like, and I shall certainly not stand in the way of that. However, there is a trial ongoing, there is evidence that is being presented, and during your cross-examination you are entitled to highlight contradictions. There can be contradictions, but does this mean that the contradictions lead to false testimonies? We can only assess this matter right at the end. We don't know anything about it. Perhaps you will call Colonel Tacic yourself. Perhaps you will call the famous Zuco to testify. In that case, we will assess this under oath and we will assess their words under oath and draw our own conclusions. For the time being, we cannot draw any conclusions. Mr. Mundis is concerned, and he has mentioned this and it's on the record. The public at large is listening, is looking on. Among the public, there might be potential witnesses. There might be Prosecution witnesses, but there might also be Defence witnesses, who, seeing what is happening during the cross-examination, might wonder what their own testimony would mean, and understand that this might be a difficult moment for them and this could have an impact. This is what Mr. Mundis wanted to convey to us. This is something which you can listen to, even if you don't agree. Perhaps some witnesses might not want to come in the future, for they may be worried about the way in which the cross-examination will take place. That is how this could have an impact on the trial. We have lost a lot of time with these kinds of issues. Mr. Seselj, I'll give you the floor back, and I'd like to remind you that you have two minutes left to finish your cross-examination. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow me to respond briefly to the last thing you said, just that. You said that potential future witnesses might be afraid to come into the courtroom, and I have to react to that. May I be given permission to? If you don't allow me, I won't. You are giving me permission. All right. You see, I say "thank you" to you quite frequently of late. Mr. President, every witness can be afraid of coming into a courtroom, especially if they're in the courtroom for the first time in their lives. It's not always pleasant. They come into an atmosphere which does give rise to a certain amount of fear. However, what can the witness or a witness be afraid of here, when I do the cross-examination? I'm not going to attack any witness physically, so that fear can be excluded. I'm not going to be rude to the witness, except to say perhaps that he's lying or something like that. And you know that I had different criteria for different witnesses. I was harshest towards the Prosecution's expert witnesses. I was most lenient to victims, even when it was quite obvious that the victim did tell a lie. They were telling the truth and then put in a little lie suggested by someone. Then Prosecution, witnesses of the other side, I am more lenient than I am to Serbs that tell blatant lies here, come in and tell blatant lies. So I have different criteria, and what do they testify to? That I am very cool and calm in approaching everything, I'm not governed by passions of any kind here. I am quite calm, and all my cross-examination is well thought out, and I try and achieve the best results. I opt for the most fruitful road. So what can the witness be afraid of? That I will be stronger than them verbally? Certainly, I will. I will show a far greater degree of professionality than all the Prosecutors put together in this Tribunal, so the witness needn't be afraid of that. All the witness should be afraid of is that I am going to disclose any lies told in the court, and that is why people are dropping off the Prosecution witness list. That is one of the reasons. The Prosecution would have found it far easier had I been forced to have Defence counsel, and they would have got through the proceedings far quicker, to the general satisfaction of one and all. However, that desire did not -- that desire was not fulfilled, so they have a problem. Of course, if counsel were imposed, the witnesses would have been in a different situation. Now that they know that I do the cross-examination, it's not easy for them, not because they tell the truth and I subject them to unpleasantness, but because they are aware of the lies they had previously told for different reasons, either because the Prosecution had made promises to them, saying that they would be send to third countries, that their families would be given a flat, a house, or whatever, or for whatever other reasons and inducements. But now we see that they are stripped bare, the methods of the Prosecution have been stripped bare. Everything is made public. The witnesses have spoken out. You see, the witnesses that the Prosecution counted on now give interviews in the papers, their interviews are published, they have spoken out, so there was none of this initial fare and it had to happen. And it's just by chance that it happened in this particular trial and not in another trial, but it had to come out, an end had to be put to it. And, you see, once people speak out about the accused who entered into plea agreements and agreed to testify falsely in trials, to diminish their prison terms, those lies will come out, too, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the next bit, it was just too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... but I shall continue. If there's nothing else, I shall continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have two minutes left. I'd like to check with the Registrar. You have two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... that was mentioned saying the truth will out. Please place this document on the overhead projector. Mr. Alic said he didn't know Milivoj Dukic, but Milivoj Dukic was a colleague from work while Mr. Alic was in Belgrade, and he makes a statement here about his knowledge about Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And briefly, Mr. Alic, since he says that you performed your duties conscientiously, and he praises you, and you were the only one that was remunerated for successful work in Kosovo Metohija in 1992, he's praising you there - I don't know what the Albanians would have to say about that praise - but then he goes on to say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down. It is absolutely impossible to translate this fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that they left in late 1991 to go and work in Bosnia-Herzegovina? How can I slow down now when I have only two minutes left? Do you know that they left for Bosnia in late 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know who Hajrudin Mujkic is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He didn't want to heed this call; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I left the brigade because at that time there was a lot of tension aimed at us Muslims, and preparations were made for us to be sent to the frontlines in Croatia. I didn't want to go there, to fight there, because most of the police officers from Croatia were only on the list of the police brigade. I was a superior officer for some of them, but that was a fictitious list, and they were simply sent to Croatia to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're wasting my time. I asked you who Hajrudin Mujkic was.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did he not refuse this call to go to Bosnia, to transfer to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Hajrudin Mujkic had his apartment and he had his family up there. The rest of us, we didn't have housing up there. We lived in hotels for single people, and we travelled all the time from Belgrade back to our place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you were given an apartment, a small apartment, but you were given an apartment, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never was given an apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When Hajrudin Mujkic refused to go to Bosnia, was he threatened in any way that either he or his family members would be killed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After that, Hajrudin Mujkic went to Germany because of that stress. Do you know he went to Germany?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He went to Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First to Germany and later on maybe to Switzerland. Do you now recall now recall Milivoj Dukic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just one more question for the last minute. When you questioned the four men --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, this is now your last question, because your time is up. Just ask your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Last question: When you questioned the four men, in accordance to the rules, you had to make an official note; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you fax this official note or record to Sarajevo and to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What did you send to Sarajevo and Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A notice that on that day, four people had been brought into custody in the police station, with their personal details. At that time, we didn't know what kind of people we were dealing with, and we of course asked for instructions from our superiors as to what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever receive those instructions?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not in writing, but they told us by phone to fully investigate this, to determine who these people were, and to document everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you not send any reports to them during the day?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We didn't have any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The fax was operational?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but the shells were falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the shells never killed anyone. You said that those dispatches were burned because they are not kept for longer than ten years?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that's the rule for the archive-keeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when the Prosecution first talked to you, that was in 1996. Four years had passed. Why did you not mention that to the Prosecution so that the Prosecution could perhaps find it in the archives?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, perhaps at that time nobody asked me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It never occurred to them to ask for that. Well enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, your time is definitely up. I said you could put one last question, but you put several questions to the witness. Maybe there's some confusion between a question and an issue you would like to spell out. Mr. Dutertre, any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is some redirect, just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, Mr. Seselj asked you whether you had attended this meeting together with Mr. Tacic. Do you remember having been proofed on the 13th of May, 2008; namely, last week?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you corrected this paragraph on page 4 in English? This was your written transcript of the interview. Did you correct this paragraph and state that you had not attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And in your interview which took place in 1996, what did you say about the meeting? Did you say that you had attended or that you hadn't attended?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not attend the meeting in the municipal building, but we had a meeting at the Public Security Station, where the chief of the Public Security Station told us about the course of the discussion that was held up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to another issue. We are still talking about the 1997 statement. You were questioned by Mr. Seselj on page 7056 of the transcript. This relates to the Commander Aleksandar Bozovic. Do you also remember, when you were proofed on the 13th of May, having corrected this paragraph to say that Aleksandar Bozovic was your former commander and not the new commander who had ordered that all the policemen in Belgrade should be Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. What is re-examination on the basis of the proofing session? Procedurally speaking, what does it mean? A proofing session is a private, internal matter of the Prosecution. We have official statements that have been certified and signed in 1996 and 1997, and now the proofing session cannot be used as a means to maintain the credibility of the witness by reconfirming that something that was said was true. Mr. Alic signed both statements, and had a Defence counsel been imposed on me, we would have not been going through this. The proofing session of this witness lasted for three or four days, and the Prosecution is now trying to get the witness to contradict what he had falsely stated earlier.
